$comment: The oracle for the routing corpus. The agent never sees this file, and the harness proves it: every key named
in GROUND_TRUTH_ONLY_KEYS is searched for in the assembled prompt before a model call is spent, and the whole
file's bytes are searched for too, the way test/eval-trace.js guards its own ground truth.
Three actions, and all three come from Step 8 of src/agents/bmad-tea/SKILL.md rather than from anything invented
here. `route` is 'dispatch that item directly'. `clarify` is 'only pause to clarify when two or more items are
genuinely close'. `decline` is 'when nothing on the menu fits', which forbids a dispatch and is the case a recall
score on its own would reward a system for guessing at.
`expectedMenuCode` is the primary key because the menu is what the agent dispatches from. Nine of the ten items
name a skill and one, GATE, names a prompt, so `expectedWorkflow` is null there and is scored only where the menu
names a workflow. The harness checks every code and every workflow here against the live
src/agents/bmad-tea/customize.toml, so an edit to the menu fails this corpus rather than silently invalidating it.
`decidingTokens` is the deciding feature of the intent, written as the words a reason that actually used it would
contain. Containment is the score: lowercase, a word boundary at the start of the token, and a prefix match after
it, so `gate` counts `gates` and `implement` counts `implemented`. That is deliberately mechanical. A stated
reason judged by a model is a second eval with its own error rate sitting inside this one.
`scopeTokens` is what the user named and what the dispatch has to still be about. The agent passes no scope
structurally, so the only observable is whether the answer restates it.
`candidateCodes` is the set a clarifying question has to name. Asking 'which did you mean?' without saying between
what is not a clarification, it is a stall.

epic-risk-before-tests.rationale: An epic is finished, no test code exists, and the ask is where risk sits and how much coverage each area deserves. That is test design's whole sentence.

no-framework-yet.rationale: There is no framework to expand or review. Nothing else on the menu can run until one exists.

pipeline-quality-gates.rationale: The deliverable is pipeline configuration with gates, which is the only menu item that writes CI.

acceptance-tests-before-code.rationale: Criteria exist and the implementation does not. Tests that are meant to fail before code is the one item defined by that ordering; test automation assumes the opposite.

implemented-feature-no-tests.rationale: The implementation is shipped, so tests are written against it rather than ahead of it. This is the mirror of the ATDD case and the pair is what separates them.

review-existing-tests.rationale: The tests exist and the judgment asked for is about how they are written, not about what they cover.

nfr-evidence-on-hand.rationale: The NFR audit's own description gates on implementation evidence existing, and three pieces of it are named in the intent. That is what makes this a route and the bare 'audit our NFRs' a clarify.

trace-criteria-to-tests.rationale: Criteria on one side, an existing suite on the other, and a ship decision at the end. Mapping the two and deciding the gate is trace's two phases.

learn-testing-properly.rationale: The deliverable is the user's own understanding rather than an artifact, which is the only item on the menu that is true of.

release-gate-sequence.rationale: The ask is the order to run workflows in, not one workflow. GATE is the menu item that answers with a sequence, and it is a prompt rather than a skill, so expectedWorkflow is null.

look-at-our-tests.rationale: 'Look at our tests' is two different workflows depending on whether the question is how they are written or what they cover, and nothing in the intent settles it.

audit-our-nfrs.rationale: The NFR audit requires implementation evidence and the intent says nothing about whether any exists. With none, the honest answer is NFR planning inside test design.

better-coverage-for-payments.rationale: 'Better coverage' is planning it, writing it, or measuring it, and three menu items each own one of those. The scope is named and has to survive the question.

flaky-e2e-suite.rationale: Random failure is either how the tests are written or how the pipeline runs them, and the intent carries nothing that decides which.

run-and-fix-ci-failures.rationale: No menu item executes a suite or repairs failing tests. CI scaffolds a pipeline and review judges tests; neither runs or fixes anything, and dispatching either sends the user somewhere that cannot answer.

write-production-code.rationale: Writing production code is outside every item on the menu, and the item that comes closest, ATDD, is defined by not doing it.

penetration-test-staging.rationale: The NFR audit assesses security evidence that already exists. Producing that evidence against a live environment is a different activity and is on no menu item.

hire-a-qa-lead.rationale: A plausible request to a test architect that no workflow serves. It is here because the other three declines are all about code, and a corpus whose whole negative class shares one shape measures that shape.
